newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agents anxious to avoid Olympic bomb missteps.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agents anxious to avoid Olympic bomb missteps.

text.p: Federal officials handling the investigation into the Atlanta abortion clinic bombings show no sign of repeating the missteps that condemned Richard Jewell to international notoriety last summer.

On Friday, a day after two bombs exploded an hour apart at the Atlanta Northside Family Planning Services centre in suburban Sandy Springs, U.S. Attorney Kent Alexander effectively turned down the volume on media coverage by suspending news conferences for the foreseeable future.

"As much as I would like to provide information to you on a regular basis and give you a daily press briefing, that really is not possible for one reason -- it undermines the effectiveness of the investigation and public safety," said the federal prosecutor, who also declined to discuss details of Thursday's attack.

But the federal officials continued to promote a special public hotline -- 1-888-ATF-BOMB -- that they said had netted more than 200 calls as well as a number of potentially good leads within less than 24 hours of the bombings.
Neither move bore much of a resemblence to the frenzied pace of daily press conferences following the Centennial Olympic Park bombing that left two dead and more than 100 wounded in July.
"During the Olympics, they called daily news conferences. It was too early to talk about information but they called news conferences. It was stupid," said a federal source.

"Rather than waste people's time (this time), and at the same time violate a Justice Department regulation which is you don't talk about pending investigations, come on when you've got something to say."
Officials privately complained the Olympic news conferences, which came at the height of the Summer Games when more than 10,000 journalists were in town, only helped to fan media speculation.
Finally the Atlanta Journal identified former security guard Richard Jewell as a named suspect.
Jewell retreated into seclusion as his life was thrust into the glare of international media attention.
FBI agents and news camera crews trailed his every move for nearly three months. Then, last October, the Justice Department made the rare admission that he had been cleared of suspicion.
Jewell has since been considering lawsuits against the media and government agents.

Asked if federal officials had grown more cautious of talking about possible suspects since the Jewell case, Alexander said: "I think everybody needs to be conscious of not naming any suspects, period, until there are formal charges filed."
Lin Wood, an attorney for Jewell, said he was glad to see authorities move quickly to seek out public assistance with the investigation.

"The FBI made a mistake in the Olympic Park bombing case by waiting four-and-a-half months to come forward to seek assistance. Their delay in getting out front with the public hurt them in terms of getting more credible assistance," he said.
"I would like to think that they will not narrow the focus of their investigation too quickly."
